items.text: Piazzolla wanted the record to sound as if half-drunk players had played it in a bordello.
items.why: Production: 'Piazzolla wrote in the liner notes of his desire to have the music sound as if it were played by "half-drunk musicians in a bordello."' Paraphrased; the reused quote is five words.
Production: 'Recorded in New York City in 1987'.

items.text: The music was first developed for a theater piece about the history of tango.
items.why: Production: 'Its music was originally developed as a theater performance about the history of the tango.'

items.text: Pablo Zinger had served as musical director for that stage production.
items.why: Production: 'Zinger had acted as the musical director for the stage production.' Note the pack flags this sentence '[ citation needed ]', so it is the weakest claim in the notes.

items.text: Piazzolla played the bandoneon and recorded with his Quinteto Tango Nuevo.
items.why: Production: 'Piazzolla, who played the bandoneon, recorded the album with his Quinteto Tango Nuevo.'

items.text: Pablo Ziegler and Pablo Zinger played piano, and Horacio Malvicino played guitar.
items.why: Production: 'Pablo Ziegler and Pablo Zinger played piano' ... 'Horacio Malvicino played guitar.'

items.text: The saxophone on Rough Dancer came from Paquito D'Rivera.
items.why: Production: 'Paquito D'Rivera played saxophone on Rough Dancer.'

items.text: Nonesuch Records put out a reissue of the album in the late 1990s.
items.why: Lead: 'The album was reissued by Nonesuch Records in the late 1990s.'

missed: How it sounds: AllMusic says that, unlike Zero Hour, it has 'more of whimsical feel' with shifts in tempo and mood handled more smoothly, and Christgau says it limits improvisatory space. listen_for is empty although the pack lists tracks such as 'Knife Fight' and 'Milonga for Three'.
